timelineEvents.title: Sons of Himalayan Rivers & Sansari Devi Worship
timelineEvents.culturalImpact: Established the sacred relationship between the Bote people and Nepal’s river ecosystems, strictly forbidding the poisoning of waters.
timelineEvents.titleNepali: संसारी देवी पूजा एवं प्राचीन जल संस्कार
timelineEvents.summary: The earliest recorded presence of Bote settlements along the Bagmati, Narayani, and Kaligandaki riverbanks. Elders performed animist river worship to Sansari Devi, requesting safe waters, rich fish harvests, and immunity from monsoon floods.

Royal decrees (Lal Mohar) formally granted the Bote community hereditary monopoly charters (Tar) to command ferry crossings across Nepal’s roaring Himalayan torrents, bridging trade between Kathmandu Valley and the southern plains.
timelineEvents.culturalImpact: Recognized Bote boatmen as indispensable state navigators, granting them tax exemptions and autonomous ghat governance.
timelineEvents.title: Royal Tar Charters & Customary Ferry Monopolies
timelineEvents.titleNepali: शाही सनद: तार अधिकार र माझी प्रथा

timelineEvents.summary: Master boatbuilders perfected the creation of single-log canoes (Ek-Dunge Nau) sculpted from giant Simal and Sal trees. Using hand adzes (chari), artisans hollowed trunks with mathematical uniform buoyancy and fire-seasoned hulls against rot.
timelineEvents.titleNepali: एक-ढुङ्गे नाउ: परम्परागत काठको डुङ्गा शिल्पी
timelineEvents.title: Architecture of Ek-Dunge Nau (Single-Log Canoe)
timelineEvents.culturalImpact: Created indigenous watercraft capable of safely navigating Class IV rapids carrying cargo, cattle, and dozens of passengers.

timelineEvents.summary: The construction of modern steel and concrete highway bridges over the Bagmati and Narayani rivers abruptly made the ancestral ferry trade obsolete. Bote families adapted by transitioning into riverbed gravel harvesting, cast-net fishing, and subsistence agriculture.
timelineEvents.culturalImpact: Spurred community introspection and the first grassroots meetings to protect indigenous linguistic identity and land claims.
timelineEvents.title: East-West Highway Construction & Bridge Disruption
timelineEvents.titleNepali: पूर्व-पश्चिम राजमार्ग र आधुनिक पुल निर्माण

timelineEvents.title: Official Janajati Indigenous Nationality Classification
timelineEvents.titleNepali: आदिवासी जनजाति उत्थान राष्ट्रिय प्रतिष्ठान सूचिकरण
timelineEvents.summary: Under the National Foundation for Development of Indigenous Nationalities (NFDIN) Act 2058, the Government of Nepal officially classified the Bote as one of the 59 distinct indigenous nationalities (Adivasi Janajati) of Nepal in the endangered category.
timelineEvents.culturalImpact: Granted formal constitutional recognition and state provisions for the safeguarding of the Bote language, customs, and educational quotas.
Began the creation of the first community-driven Tarahi Bote lexicon and oral folklore audio archives.
artifacts: Audio tape reels of elder folktales
timelineEvents.title: National Census & Tarahi Bote Dialect Documentation
timelineEvents.titleNepali: राष्ट्रिय जनगणना र तराही बोटे भाषा अनुसन्धान
timelineEvents.summary: The National Population Census recorded 11,258 Bote community members, highlighting core concentrations in Sarlahi, Chitwan, and Nawalpur. Linguistic researchers and community elders initiated phonological studies on the endangered Tarahi Bote oral dialect.

Youth leaders in Karmaiya convened the national assembly to establish Bote Youth Community Nepal (BoteYouthCommunityNepal). Under Chairman Navaraj Bot and the Youth Council, initiatives encompass annual higher-education scholarships, Bagmati river ecology cleanups, and digital web preservation.
timelineEvents.culturalImpact: Uniting 10 executive leaders across youth and elder councils to bridge ancestral river reverence with modern professional opportunities.
timelineEvents.titleNepali: बोटे युवा समुदाय नेपाल स्थापना र नयाँ नेतृत्व
timelineEvents.title: Founding of Bote Youth Community Nepal (BYCN)

culturalTraditions.title: Sansari Devi River Puja & Boat Racing
culturalTraditions.titleNepali: संसारी देवी नदी पूजा र डुङ्गा दौड
rituals: Elder chants invoking river deities before dawn
Sanctification of traditional dugout wooden boats with vermillion and ceremonial flags
Competitive canoe race between Bote youth teams across district ghats
Communal feast featuring clay-pot river fish and local rice
culturalTraditions.significance: Protects boat operators and fishers from whirlpools and natural disasters while reinforcing clan solidarity.
culturalTraditions.description: The supreme spiritual assembly of the Bote community. Families gather on the banks of the Bagmati and Narayani rivers to worship Sansari Devi (Goddess of the Universe) and aquatic spirits. Elders offer red vermillion, flowers, and milk into the currents to ensure tranquil waters, safe boating lanes, and protection from monsoon floods.

culturalTraditions.title: Ek-Dunge Nau: Traditional Dugout Canoe Architecture
rituals: Prayer to the forest spirits before tree harvesting
Precision adze carving and uniform thickness balance testing
Controlled fire-charring inside the hull to seal wood pores against decay
culturalTraditions.titleNepali: एक-ढुङ्गे नाउ: परम्परागत काठको डुङ्गा शिल्पी
culturalTraditions.significance: Demonstrates deep traditional ecological knowledge and woodworking heritage dating back centuries.
culturalTraditions.description: The Bote canoe is an architectural marvel of indigenous woodworking. Carved from a single massive trunk of Simal (silk-cotton) or Sal timber, artisans use adzes (chari) to hollow out the hull uniformly so the boat remains buoyant and balanced through turbulent Himalayan river rapids.

rituals: Holy river dip at Bagmati Ghat at sunrise
Offering of sesame and wild river herbs to departed elders
Folk singing of river legends with Khainjadi drums
culturalTraditions.titleNepali: माघे सङ्क्रान्ति र नदी किनार पितृ तर्पण
culturalTraditions.title: Maghe Sankranti Ancestral River Offerings
culturalTraditions.significance: Celebrates the transition of the sun, family reunions, and homage to river ancestral souls.
culturalTraditions.description: On Maghe Sankranti, Bote community members wake before sunrise to take ritual baths in the sacred rivers. They offer prayers to ancestors, consume forest sweet potatoes (Tarul), sesame sweets, and organize riverbank archery and dugout rowing demonstrations.

culturalTraditions.titleNepali: चोया र कुशबाट माछा मार्ने खुङ्ग्री तथा डोको निर्माण
culturalTraditions.significance: Eco-friendly, biodegradable fishing gear exemplifying sustainable indigenous aquatic harvesting.
rituals: Seasonal harvesting of mature river reeds
Soaking and splitting bamboo fibers into pliable strands
Weaving distinct mesh gradients according to river current strength
culturalTraditions.title: Choya Grass Weaving & Fishing Trap Craft
culturalTraditions.description: Harvesting wild elephant grass (choya and khar) along the river floodplains, Bote artisans weave specialized conical fish traps (Khungri) and storage baskets (Dhoko, Dala). These traps allow river water to flow freely while capturing specific adult fish without harming juveniles.

features: Wide waist-sash (Patuka) providing back support during heavy basket carrying
Dark earthy dye tones resistant to river silt staining
dressItems.significance: Provides thermal ease in humid inner-Terai river valleys while upholding distinct indigenous modesty.
dressItems.materials: Handwoven coarse cotton, dyed in deep red, indigo blue, or dark black borders.
dressItems.name: Bote Gunya & Cholo (Women's Wrap Attire)
dressItems.description: The Gunya is a traditional cotton wrap skirt draped gracefully slightly above the ankles, allowing women to wade into river waters while fishing or washing without soaking the hem. It is paired with a snug, contrasting red or blue cotton blouse (Cholo) and tied at the waist with a Patuka sash.

dressItems.materials: Lightweight handloom khadi cotton and wool-blend waistcoat.
dressItems.significance: Optimized for agility in rapid river currents and single-log boat navigation.
dressItems.name: Traditional Dhoti & Waistcoat (Men's Attire)
dressItems.description: Bote men wear a short cotton loincloth or dhoti tied securely above the knees for unrestricted rowing and net casting. Over the torso, they wear a breathable bhoto (undershirt) and an open waistcoat with inner utility pockets for holding fishing hooks and tobacco.
features: Short knee-length wrap allowing athletic rowing balance
Utility waistcoat designed for carrying river tools
Head cloth (Gamcha) for protection against blistering sun

dressItems.name: Hansuli & Silver Ornaments (Jewelry Heritage)
dressItems.significance: Symbols of marital grace, generational inheritance, and spiritual protection from water spirits.
features: Hansuli: Solid hand-forged silver neck collar
dressItems.materials: Pure silver, brass, and sacred glass bead strands (Pote).
dressItems.description: During Sansari Puja, weddings, and communal assemblies, Bote women adorn themselves with heavy silver ornaments. The Hansuli is a solid, torc-like silver neckband sitting high on the collarbone, complemented by ornate nose rings (Bulaki) and carved silver anklets (Kalli).

costumes.name: Traditional Riverman Attire (Dhoti, Kachhad & Bhewa)
costumes.culturalSignificance: Symbol of river mastery and ecological harmony. Designed specifically over centuries for aquatic livelihoods and tropical Terai climate.
costumes.description: The ancient everyday riverine attire worn by Bote boatmen and fishermen along the Bagmati, Narayani, and Kali Gandaki rivers. The Kachhad is wrapped securely above the knees to allow unrestricted motion when navigating swift river rapids and poling dugout canoes (Ek-Dunge Nau).

costumes.description: A deeply revered traditional Bote feminine attire featuring a wrapped Gunya ankle skirt, a form-fitted cotton Cholo blouse, and a thick Patuka waist binder that protects the lumbar back during long hours of riverbank net hauling and paddy cultivation.
